content: The earliest evidence of cancer can be traced back to ancient Egyptian literature, around 3000 BC. This is documented in the Edwin Smith Papyrus, which describes eight cases of breast tumors treated by cauterization using a tool called the fire drill. In 1761, Giovanni Morgagni of Padua became the first to perform autopsies that linked illnesses to specific pathological findings. John Hunter, a Scottish surgeon (1728–1793), proposed that cancer could be surgically removed if the tumor had not invaded surrounding tissues and was still movable. He also suggested in the 1700s that tumors might originate from lymphatic fluid constantly excreted by the blood. In the 19th century, Rudolf Virchow was the first to correlate diseases with microscopic pathology, advancing the understanding of cancer at the cellular level. Two Dutch physicians, Zacutus Lusitani (1575–1642) and Nicholas Tulp (1593–1674), published works in 1649 and 1652, respectively, suggesting that breast cancer might be contagious based on their observations of tumor occurrences within members of the same household. In the 1990s, the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes were identified as being associated with an increased risk of developing breast cancer. In 1713, Bernardino Ramazzini, an Italian physician, reported a higher incidence of breast cancer among nuns, highlighting a potential link between the disease and hormonal factors. Modern mammography techniques were developed in the late 1960s, and by 1976, the American Cancer Society officially recommended mammography as a screening tool. In the late 19th century, William Stewart Halsted, a professor of surgery at Johns Hopkins University, introduced the radical mastectomy procedure for breast cancer treatment. In 1719, Lorenz Heister, a German surgeon, wrote about his ideas for mastectomy and lumpectomy in his book Chirurgie. In 1896, Thomas Beatson, a graduate of the University of Edinburgh, described the relationship between oophorectomy (surgical removal of the ovaries) and breast cancer, laying the foundation for hormonal therapy in breast cancer treatment. In the 1970s, clinical trials demonstrated that less extensive surgeries were equally effective for most women with breast cancer, leading to a shift in surgical approaches. During the final decades of the 20th century, techniques were developed to minimize the removal of normal tissue during tumor excision. In the late 1990s, trastuzumab (Herceptin), the first therapeutic monoclonal antibody, was approved for the treatment of breast cancer.
